headline: High-risk shared filesystem and broad egress create prompt-injection, leakage, and cascading-action exposure between Goose and oh-my-openagent.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Goose reads/writes the user filesystem and uses MCP; oh-my-openagent also touches project files and runtime-injected MCPs/hooks. That creates a plausible default bridge where one agent can place instructions in files the other ingests. The interaction is documented by both profiles, though not directly reproduced.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same workspace or config directory
IF either agent parses file content or MCP payloads as instructions without provenance checks
mitigations: Separate workspaces per agent
Disable shared MCP endpoints
Add provenance tags to files exchanged between agents
Require manual review of any cross-agent file before execution

B_data_leakage.rationale: Both agents touch project code and session/history-like data, and both have broad network egress. Goose explicitly handles model-provider keys and extension tokens; oh-my-openagent handles provider auth prompts and sends data to external services. Shared files or logs could leak sensitive content across the pair in default use.
conditions: IF the agents share a workspace, cache, or logs
IF either agent uploads file contents or session history to external APIs
mitigations: Use separate OS users
Exclude secrets and auth files from shared directories
Turn off automatic upload of workspace files
Rotate any exposed provider tokens immediately

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Goose can write the filesystem, modify git state, and run shell commands; oh-my-openagent can also access files and spawn subprocesses with full-permissions mode. On a shared workspace, concurrent writes and git mutations can race and corrupt state. The profiles support this pathway directly, so uncertainty does not reduce severity.
conditions: IF both agents are active in the same repository or directory
IF either agent performs git commits, rebases, or file rewrites without locking
mitigations: Run only one writer at a time
Use per-agent branches
Enable filesystem locking around shared paths
Keep one agent read-only for the session

D_cascading_error.rationale: Goose can generate code and act through shell/MCP tools, while oh-my-openagent can use runtime-injected MCPs and hooks plus browser/subprocess access. If one agent's output is fed into the other without verification, errors can cascade into real actions or commits. Both profiles show an action-capable chain, so the blast radius is not just informational.
conditions: IF oh-my-openagent consumes Goose output as authoritative
IF Goose executes or commits based on oh-my-openagent summaries without review
mitigations: Insert a human approval step between agents
Require source citations for any factual claim
Disable auto-execution of generated commands
Limit one agent to drafting only

E_compliance.rationale: Both profiles indicate handling of provider authentication data and broad network egress, but neither documents residency or regulated-data certifications. The compliance risk is therefore a mismatch in retention or data-transfer policy rather than a proven breach. Because the pair can move project code and auth material to external services, the safer choice is medium.
conditions: IF regulated data or secrets are placed in shared prompts or files
IF either agent sends those materials to third-party APIs
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of both agents
Review vendor retention settings
Disable telemetry where possible
Use redacted test data only
